units.text: According to Tapia-Rojas et al. (2013), in cultivated and pristine soils, beetles feeding on roots are beneficial as they help improve soil structure by favouring water and airflow. In doing so, they incorporate their excreta, which is rich in assimilable nitrogen and abundant microorganisms that benefit plants. Therefore, Romero-López et al. (2010) argued that the work performed by these species contributes to (i) increasing soil porosity, drainage and aeration by behaving similarly to earthworms and positively influencing the physical characteristics of the soil; (ii) improving soil chemical properties by immobilising and distributing nutrients, as well as mineralizing and/or humifying organic matter, thus functioning as biological catalysts and (iii) stimulating various soil biological activities, enhancing the microbiological decomposition of organic matter, regulating biotic composition and exporting some soil nutrients in their adult phase to the upper soil subsystem. Considering the aforementioned, identifying meaningful traits of rooteating scarab beetles and assessing their role in soils will allow us to understand and quantify their contribution of bioturbation in landscapes with land use changes.

Cetoniines and rutelines have saprophagous members in their larval stage that exploit resources, such as soil organic matter, leaf litter or decomposing logs (Deloya et al., 1995; Morón & Deloya, 2002; Neita-Moreno et al., 2006). Although adult Cetoniinae have specialised jaws for consuming soft foods, such as nectar, sap, pollen and ripe fruit, the larvae are characterised by strong jaws that aid in the decomposition of plant-derived organic matter (Deloya & Gasca-Alvarez, ´ 2018). Larvae of beetles from Rutelinae, Dynastinae and Cetoniinae have been found in association with ant refuse dumps of the genera Atta Fabricius (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) and Acromyrmex Mayr (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) (Navarrete-Heredia, 2001), and larvae of Cetoniinae have been reported in nests of Cornitermes Wasmann (Isoptera: Termitidae) and Dwersitermes (Silvestri) (Isoptera: Termitidae) termites (Puker et al., 2012), likely taking advantage of the microclimatic conditions and food (mostly faeces) generated in these spaces beneath the soil surface. In an experiment conducted by Micó et al. (2011), the larvae of a Cetonia species were able to degrade wood in a way that produced nutrient-rich residues with easily decomposable lignin. This facilitates the decomposition of detritus by other saprophagous organisms, thus contributing to the carbon cycling system. In contrast, rutelines are commonly found on fallen logs, feeding on partially decomposed wood or accumulated detritus (Morón et al., 1997). However, in this group, identification from immature stages can be complex, so the recognition of their contribution to this function in the larval stage is still limited.
